rv.q: The theatrical structure Fish has built is something like an evidence board for the mind, where each new echo can be pinned up and examined and connections both clinical and intuitive can be made.

Elektra draws its centrifugal power from the harmony at its core, and the harshly beautiful, straight-tone Balkan belt of these six vocalists pierces as brazenly as Elektra’s own howling in the darkness.
The acting ensemble is uniformly dynamic.

Whatever one thinks about the production's oddities, however, it is Benko's triumph, serving as a notice that despite her busy career, she is a seriously underused talent, ready, willing, and able to take on the most challenging roles.
The ensemble delivers Carson’s sharp-edged, propulsive verse with an unadorned clarity.
Overall, though, Mr. Fish’s interpretation may leave you more mystified than entertained.
Daniel Fish’s Elektra, on the other hand, has been drained of all its power.
Together, these talented artists have made this Elektra relevant, thought-provoking, and, most importantly, worthy of discussion.
Elektra is a frustrating experience because there’s so much here that’s compelling without the directorial overreach.
There’s enough in the production to make it unique and unnerving without going to such lengths.
Fish’s work is always mind-blowing, but with Elektra, that is both positive and negative.

cn.t: Critics are split on Daniel Fish's stark, concept-heavy *Elektra*—some find his modern impositions distracting, others praise the boldness. Tina Benko's fierce performance and Ted Hearne's a cappella score earn near-universal acclaim.

vr.q: If you enjoy more experimental theater, if you more like the art of theater than the entertainment, then I think Electra will appeal to you.
